cards.explanation: Dominance describes the relationship between alleles for a phenotype, not which allele is more common.
cards.text: Under complete dominance, the heterozygote expresses the {{c1::dominant phenotype}}.
cards.question: Under complete dominance, the heterozygote expresses the {{c1::dominant phenotype}}.

cards.explanation: Each gamete normally carries one allele at a diploid locus.
cards.text: Separation of the two alleles into different gametes is Mendel's law of {{c1::segregation}}.
cards.question: Separation of the two alleles into different gametes is Mendel's law of {{c1::segregation}}.

cards.explanation: Closely linked loci can be inherited together more frequently than independent assortment predicts.
cards.text: Independent assortment applies most directly to {{c1::unlinked loci}}.
cards.question: Independent assortment applies most directly to {{c1::unlinked loci}}.

cards.explanation: The flower example contrasts an intermediate phenotype with expression of both phenotypes.
cards.text: A heterozygote intermediate between both homozygotes shows {{c1::incomplete dominance}}.
cards.question: A heterozygote intermediate between both homozygotes shows {{c1::incomplete dominance}}.

cards.explanation: It is different from an intermediate blended phenotype.
cards.text: Expression of both alleles' distinguishable products in a heterozygote is {{c1::codominance}}.
cards.question: Expression of both alleles' distinguishable products in a heterozygote is {{c1::codominance}}.

cards.explanation: This concerns interactions between loci rather than dominance within one locus.
cards.text: An interaction in which one gene modifies or masks another locus is {{c1::epistasis}}.
cards.question: An interaction in which one gene modifies or masks another locus is {{c1::epistasis}}.

cards.explanation: Multifactorial inheritance additionally emphasises environmental contributions.
cards.text: A trait influenced by many loci is {{c1::polygenic}}.
cards.question: A trait influenced by many loci is {{c1::polygenic}}.

cards.explanation: These are conventional chart symbols, not a full account of gender or chromosomal biology.
cards.text: The conventional pedigree symbol for a male is a {{c1::square}}.
cards.question: The conventional pedigree symbol for a male is a {{c1::square}}.

cards.explanation: Interpret the legend because particular pedigrees may use additional shading conventions.
cards.text: An affected individual is conventionally shown using a {{c1::filled symbol}}.
cards.question: An affected individual is conventionally shown using a {{c1::filled symbol}}.

cards.explanation: It does not by itself identify cause of death.
cards.text: A diagonal slash across a pedigree symbol indicates a {{c1::deceased individual}}.
cards.question: A diagonal slash across a pedigree symbol indicates a {{c1::deceased individual}}.

cards.explanation: The parents share ancestry, increasing the chance of sharing a rare recessive allele.
cards.text: A double partner line conventionally indicates {{c1::consanguinity}}.
cards.question: A double partner line conventionally indicates {{c1::consanguinity}}.

cards.explanation: It does not prescribe an exact sequence or number of affected children.
cards.text: A Punnett square predicts offspring {{c1::genotype probabilities}}.
cards.question: A Punnett square predicts offspring {{c1::genotype probabilities}}.

cards.explanation: Combining one gamete from each parent fills each offspring-genotype cell.
cards.text: The outside of a Punnett square lists parental {{c1::gametes}}.
cards.question: The outside of a Punnett square lists parental {{c1::gametes}}.

cards.explanation: The variants need not be identical; compound heterozygosity is possible.
cards.text: An autosomal-recessive phenotype generally requires disease-associated variants in {{c1::both copies of the gene}}.
cards.question: An autosomal-recessive phenotype generally requires disease-associated variants in {{c1::both copies of the gene}}.

cards.explanation: The four equally probable combinations are AA, Aa, aA and aa.
cards.text: For Aa × Aa, the probability of an affected aa child is {{c1::1/4}} per pregnancy.
cards.question: For Aa × Aa, the probability of an affected aa child is {{c1::1/4}} per pregnancy.

cards.explanation: This is an unconditional probability among all children.
cards.text: For Aa × Aa, the probability of a heterozygous carrier child is {{c1::1/2}}.
cards.question: For Aa × Aa, the probability of a heterozygous carrier child is {{c1::1/2}}.

cards.explanation: Exclude aa; two of the three remaining equally likely outcomes are carriers.
cards.text: Among unaffected children of Aa × Aa, the carrier probability is {{c1::2/3}}.
cards.question: Among unaffected children of Aa × Aa, the carrier probability is {{c1::2/3}}.

cards.explanation: One affected child does not use up the affected outcome in a Punnett square.
cards.text: Each pregnancy's Mendelian risk is {{c1::independent of previous outcomes}}.
cards.question: Each pregnancy's Mendelian risk is {{c1::independent of previous outcomes}}.

cards.explanation: This pattern is suggestive, not proof; small pedigrees and other mechanisms can resemble it.
cards.text: Unaffected parents with affected children can suggest {{c1::autosomal-recessive inheritance}}.
cards.question: Unaffected parents with affected children can suggest {{c1::autosomal-recessive inheritance}}.

cards.explanation: Related individuals are more likely to share alleles inherited from an ancestor.
cards.text: Consanguinity can increase the chance that parents carry the same {{c1::rare recessive allele}}.
cards.question: Consanguinity can increase the chance that parents carry the same {{c1::rare recessive allele}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture also lists sickle cell disease and phenylketonuria.
cards.text: Cystic fibrosis is a standard example of {{c1::autosomal-recessive inheritance}}.
cards.question: Cystic fibrosis is a standard example of {{c1::autosomal-recessive inheritance}}.

cards.explanation: Penetrance and expressivity can alter whether and how the phenotype appears.
cards.text: One disease-associated allele can be sufficient for an {{c1::autosomal-dominant phenotype}}.
cards.question: One disease-associated allele can be sufficient for an {{c1::autosomal-dominant phenotype}}.

cards.explanation: This is the simple fully penetrant dominant model illustrated in the lecture.
cards.text: For an affected Aa parent and unaffected aa parent, each child has a {{c1::1/2}} chance of inheriting A.
cards.question: For an affected Aa parent and unaffected aa parent, each child has a {{c1::1/2}} chance of inheriting A.

cards.explanation: This is typical of dominant inheritance, but new variants or reduced penetrance can alter the pattern.
cards.text: Affected individuals in successive generations suggest {{c1::vertical transmission}}.
cards.question: Affected individuals in successive generations suggest {{c1::vertical transmission}}.

cards.explanation: A father passes his Y, rather than his X, to a typical XY son.
cards.text: Father-to-son transmission can support {{c1::autosomal}} rather than X-linked inheritance.
cards.question: Father-to-son transmission can support {{c1::autosomal}} rather than X-linked inheritance.

cards.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolaemia and achondroplasia are other lecture examples.
cards.text: Huntington disease illustrates {{c1::autosomal-dominant inheritance}}.
cards.question: Huntington disease illustrates {{c1::autosomal-dominant inheritance}}.

cards.explanation: One disease-associated allele may therefore be sufficient.
cards.text: X-linked recessive disease is often expressed in XY individuals because they are {{c1::hemizygous}} for most X-linked loci.
cards.question: X-linked recessive disease is often expressed in XY individuals because they are {{c1::hemizygous}} for most X-linked loci.

cards.explanation: This explains the absence of ordinary father-to-son X-linked transmission.
cards.text: A father does not transmit his X chromosome to his {{c1::sons}} in the usual XX/XY model.
cards.question: A father does not transmit his X chromosome to his {{c1::sons}} in the usual XX/XY model.

cards.explanation: This is different from homozygosity, which describes two matching alleles.
cards.text: Possessing only one copy of a locus is termed {{c1::hemizygosity}}.
cards.question: Possessing only one copy of a locus is termed {{c1::hemizygosity}}.

cards.explanation: Haemophilia A and common red–green colour-vision deficiency are additional examples.
cards.text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an example of {{c1::X-linked recessive inheritance}}.
cards.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an example of {{c1::X-linked recessive inheritance}}.

cards.explanation: Condition on the child being a son; the chance among all births differs if sex probabilities are included.
cards.text: For a carrier mother and unaffected father, each son has a {{c1::1/2}} chance of an X-linked recessive disorder.
cards.question: For a carrier mother and unaffected father, each son has a {{c1::1/2}} chance of an X-linked recessive disorder.

cards.explanation: The father supplies a normal X in this simplified model.
cards.text: For a carrier mother and unaffected father, each daughter has a {{c1::1/2}} chance of being a carrier.
cards.question: For a carrier mother and unaffected father, each daughter has a {{c1::1/2}} chance of being a carrier.

cards.explanation: This assumes typical XX/XY inheritance and that he carries the allele on his X.
cards.text: An affected father transmits his X-linked dominant allele to {{c1::all daughters}}.
cards.question: An affected father transmits his X-linked dominant allele to {{c1::all daughters}}.

cards.explanation: Both sons and daughters can inherit it.
cards.text: A heterozygous mother transmits an X-linked dominant allele to {{c1::half of children on average}}.
cards.question: A heterozygous mother transmits an X-linked dominant allele to {{c1::half of children on average}}.

cards.explanation: The source uses fragile X as an example with complex expression; it is not a simple fully penetrant Punnett-square phenotype.
cards.text: Variable severity among people with the same inherited disorder is {{c1::variable expressivity}}.
cards.question: Variable severity among people with the same inherited disorder is {{c1::variable expressivity}}.

cards.explanation: This can make an apparently unaffected person part of a dominant transmission chain.
cards.text: Failure of some allele carriers to show the phenotype is {{c1::reduced penetrance}}.
cards.question: Failure of some allele carriers to show the phenotype is {{c1::reduced penetrance}}.

cards.explanation: In the usual inheritance model, daughters do not inherit the paternal Y.
cards.text: A Y-linked allele follows the {{c1::father-to-son}} lineage.
cards.question: A Y-linked allele follows the {{c1::father-to-son}} lineage.

cards.explanation: The final unkeyed exercise pedigrees are practice material. No unverified answer or carrier probability has been guessed from small diagrams.
cards.text: An inheritance pattern should be inferred from the {{c1::whole pedigree}} rather than one affected person.
cards.question: An inheritance pattern should be inferred from the {{c1::whole pedigree}} rather than one affected person.

slides.topic: Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 3
slides.text:
What is Mendelian?


Complete Dominance & Recessiveness
The effect of one allele in a heterozygous genotype completely masks the effect of the other. The allele that masks are considered dominant to the other allele, and the masked allele is considered recessive.

slides.topic: Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 4
slides.text:
Mendel’s laws of Inheritance



Pea plant experiments led to the formation of Mendel’s Laws widely known as the Laws of Inheritance, which are:

Law of Segregation
Law of Independent Assortment
Law of Dominance

slides.topic: Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 5
slides.text:
Law of Segregation


Every organism has two alleles for each trait, and these alleles separate during meiosis, resulting in each gamete carrying only one of the alleles. Consequently, an offspring inherits a pair of alleles for a trait by receiving one allele from each parent.

slides.topic: Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 6
slides.text:
Law of independent assortment


Unlinked or distantly linked segregating gene pairs operate independently. Alleles for different traits are transmitted independently of each other. The selection of an allele for one trait does not influence the selection of an allele for another trait.

slides.topic: Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 7
Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 8
slides.text:
Law of Dominance


When the two alleles of an inherited pair are different, this is known as a heterozygous condition. One allele, which defines the organism's appearance, is referred to as the dominant allele, while the other allele, which does not have a visible impact on the organism's appearance, is termed the recessive allele.

Autosomal Dominant




The autosomal dominant allele is rare!
Affected individuals more likely to be heterozygous.
Homozygous most likely fail to survive.

slides.topic: Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 24
slides.text: In order to have an autosomal dominant disorder, only one copy of the gene (inherited from either parent) needs to contain a disease-causing mutation

slides.topic: Modes of Inheritance — Pedigrees & Risk — source 25
slides.text:
Punnett square for autosomal dominant conditions



The affected parent can pass either a disease allele or a normal allele to his/her children.

Half of the children will be heterozygotes and will express the disease.

Half will be unaffected homozygotes (On average).

Phenotype tend to appear in every generation. 
Affected offspring have at least one affected parent.

X-linked recessive



More frequently in males than in females,  WHY?
Males have only one X chromosome. A single recessive gene on that X chromosome will cause the disease

Affected males are usually born to unaffected  mothers who are carriers, the trait skips generations.

Not passed from father to son, WHY?
Males take only Y chromosome from their father
